newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Investors bullish on Indonesia's banking stocks.
newsitem.headline: Investors bullish on Indonesia's banking stocks.

text.p: Indonesia's banking stocks offer investors good scope for profits on prospects of healthy future earnings and a plan to merge state banks, analysts said at the weekend.
They said a declining trend in deposit rates combined with relatively stable lending rates, indicating higher profit margins, had lifted sentiment on banking stocks in the last few months.
Lin Che Wei, research director of Socgen Crosby Indonesia, said there was little doubt that Indonesia's economy was healthy.
"Indonesia is moving in the right direction. That's why I am very bullish on Indonesian banking stocks," he told Reuters.
Wei said that Indonesia's monetary policy was easy to predict and increased credibility of the country's macroeconomic managers.
"They try to stimulate growth but maintain very close attention to financial stability. They do not rock the boat," he said.
Daisy Chee, an analyst for UBS Securities, said buoyant economic growth, together with successful bank equity raisings, will continue to drive Indonesian bank earnings.

"With barriers to entry protecting the domestic banking industry until at least the year 2003, when the ASEAN Free Trade Area comes into force, the present domestic banking industry has some time to run," Chee said in a report.

The free trade zone aims to break down blocks to trade among the members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, which currently counts Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei as members. Burma, Laos and Cambodia are set to join soon.

Crosby's Wei also said government plans to merge the country's seven state banks into four entities should be perceived as a signal that it would boost efficiency in the banking sector and in the economy overall.
Last week, Indonesian Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad confirmed the government was studying the possibility of merging some state banks to improve competitiveness but gave no details.
Currently, Bank Negara Indonesia is the only state-controlled bank listed on the Jakarta exchange.

"By consolidating the current seven state banks, I do believe it's easier both for the central bank and the finance ministry to control the banks and reduce redundancy as currently those banks are duplicating the same resources," Wei said.
"If you have a stronger banking system, everyone will benefit," he added. "If state banks are stronger then the private banks will also be perceived as better," he added.
"Current Indonesian interest rates are extremely high because of inefficiency in the banking industry. That's why the manufacturing sectors has not grown as expected," he said.
Despite optimistism on banks' prospective earnings, both Wei and Chee agreed that the cost to income ratio of Indonesian banks remained high compared to the banking industry in the region.
"If you look at how efficient Indonesian banks are relative to other countries, the cost to income ratio is still 50 to 55, which is very high," Wei said.
Chee linked the lack of appropriate systems, banking technology and skilled staff to the higher operating costs.
